01 · Organizational diagnosis

Organizational Diagnosis - Wine & Cheese Shop

Organizational Diagnosis

Led a team in conducting interviews to assess business needs and identify opportunities to improve hiring, onboarding, and training processes. Developed recommendation for refining application questions to better align candidate qualifications with role requirements and organizational values. Managed project milestones using Asana and presented recommendations to the business owner.

Challenge

Opportunities to improve the shop’s hiring, onboarding, and training processes.

Approach

A team-led interview process to assess business needs, with project milestones managed in Asana.

Recommendations

A job analysis, plus streamlined systems and processes: mission and vision, staff meetings and 1:1s, a knowledge pre-test, visual aids, and handbook updates.

01

Interview

Assess business needs

Led a team in conducting interviews to assess the business’s needs and identify opportunities to improve its hiring, onboarding, and training processes. Project milestones were managed using Asana.

Focus areas
  • Hiring
  • Onboarding
  • Training
02

Recommend

Two areas of change

Developed two sets of recommendations, including a recommendation for refining application questions so that candidate qualifications better align with role requirements and organizational values.

Recommendation 1
Perform a job analysis

A job analysis would help with:

  • Role clarity
  • Employee expectations
  • Performance management
  • Recruitment and selection, including an application and interview guide
Recommendation 2
Streamline systems and processes

Update and standardize how the organization operates day to day:

  • Update and clarify the company mission and vision
  • Implement monthly staff meetings and 1:1s with employees
  • Implement a pre-test for wine and cheese knowledge
  • Implement visual aids and handbook modifications: safety protocols, food safety, training and onboarding processes
03

Deliver the proposal

Present to the owner

Presented the recommendations to the business owner and provided a full proposal with recommended next steps, suggested edits of content, sample agendas, and templates.

Samples from the proposal
Additional resources provided
  1. BOOKThe Five Dysfunctions of a Team: A Leadership Fable
    Patrick Lencioni
  2. BOOKGlad We Met: The Art and Science of 1:1 Meetings
    Steven G. Rogelberg
  3. TEAM BUILDINGA local team-building opportunity
Outcome / The owner received a full proposal with recommended next steps, suggested content edits, sample agendas, and templates, along with two book recommendations and a local team-building opportunity.

01

Interview

Identify needs

Interviewed the Chief Exhibitions Officer and the museum’s affiliate groups to identify the needs of the organization.

02

Map the stakeholders

Visualize relationships

Identified and visually mapped out the key stakeholders within the affiliate groups and the museum.

Analyze

03 · Organizational diagnosis

Organizational Diagnosis - Bowling Alley

Organizational Diagnosis

Interviewed leadership and employees to identify operational challenges in scheduling events, customer communication and internal knowledge gaps. Developed a low-cost, automated request form to standardize the event scheduling workflow. Streamlined staff and customer communication through automated email confirmations, request tracking and FAQ content.

Challenge

Event scheduling miscommunication: key details were missed, requests were lost, and some events were approved without review.

Approach

Interviews with the owner and employees to uncover pain points and the information the team needs to prepare for events.

Solution

A low-cost Google Form and Sheet workflow with automated confirmations, request tracking, and website FAQs.

01

Interview

Understand the problem

Interviewed the owner and employees to understand the alley’s main challenges. Miscommunication around event scheduling emerged as the biggest pain point, and it became the owner’s focus for the project.

What I learned
  • Specific details are needed up front. The team needs them to prepare the space and order food ahead of time.
  • The owner finalized every request because critical information was often missed. Employees left sticky notes asking the owner to contact customers and confirm dates.
  • The handoff broke down. The owner tried having employees gather general information, but they didn’t always collect everything, and sticky notes were sometimes misplaced.
  • Some events were approved without the owner reviewing them.
02

Create content

Standardize the request

Created an event request form so every request captures the information the team needs, collected in the same way every time.

Event request form fields
  1. Name (first and last)
  2. Email address
  3. Phone number
  4. Preferred event date
  5. Preferred time slot (e.g., 12–2 PM, 3–5 PM)
  6. Type of event (birthday, corporate, school outing, other)
  7. Estimated number of guests
  8. Age range of guests (if applicable)
  9. Preferred party package (if any)
  10. Special requests or questions
03

Recommend

Compile options for the owner

Compiled recommendations for the owner, starting with two options for the scheduling and event request workflow.

Two workflow options
Option 1Recommended
Google Form + Google Sheet

A simple, low-cost system. The form is reached through a QR code on the website, flyers, or at the front desk.

Benefits
  • No upfront cost
  • Easy to implement and maintain
  • Keeps control in-house
  • Scalable as volume grows
  • Can be enhanced later with automation (e.g., Google Apps Script)
Option 2
Commercial scheduling platform

A paid event scheduling or party-booking tool (e.g., Calendly, Acuity, Jane).

Pros
  • Professional interface
  • Some automation and calendar integration
  • May offer payment processing
Cons
  • Monthly fees
  • May not fit the alley’s specific needs (e.g., lane availability, party packages)
  • Customization may require technical support or added cost
How Option 1 works
  1. STEP 1Customer scans the QR code and fills out the request form (name, date/time, party size, contact info, etc.).
  2. STEP 2Responses populate a dedicated tab in a Google Sheet.
  3. STEP 3An automated email goes to:
    • The shared mailbox or all three points of contact, for review
    • The customer, confirming receipt and that someone will follow up within 24 hours
  4. STEP 4A staff member contacts the customer to finalize details.
Additional recommendations
  • Update the website with event scheduling information and FAQs.
  • Send an automated email after each request, letting the customer know a team member will contact them to confirm availability.
  • How to book an event
  • Cancellation policy
  • Food & drink policies
  • What’s included in event packages
  • Age limits & supervision rules
  • Event package pricing
Recommendation / Start with Option 1. It carries low risk and low cost, and it gives the business full control of its event scheduling process.
04 · Job analysis

Job Analysis - Automotive Company

Job Analysis & Redesign

Led a team of 4 to analyze job roles, identify key KSAOs, and developed recommendations for enhancing selection and training methods. Presented findings and actionable solutions, including job aids and a math selection test to the VP of HR and leadership team.

Situation

High turnover rate for Compaction Operators.

Complication

Turnover results in high costs to the company for training, onboarding, and more.

Resolution

Job analysis of the compaction operator job to refine selection and training methods.

Potential impact

Increased retention.

01

Analyze the job

C-JAM method

Used a Combination Job Analysis (C-JAM) method to analyze the Compaction Operator position: what gets done, how it gets done, and what human attributes are needed for the job. The analysis supports clarity in both selection and training.

Methodology roadmap
By the numbers
70+task statements generated
55KSAOs generated
18 / 16KSAOs rated for selection / training
02

Identify tasks and KSAOs

Findings

Interviewed subject matter experts to obtain job tasks, and obtained the KSAOs (Knowledge, Skills, Abilities, and Other characteristics) a person needs to perform the specific job. Task statements and KSAOs were identified and refined.

The task and KSAO rating patterns were then leveraged in:

  • Job description
  • Job announcement
  • Training material
  • Onboarding material
Samples from the findings
03

Recommend

Put the KSAOs to work

Developed recommendations for enhancing selection and training methods.

  1. RECOMMENDATION 1Incorporate KSAOs in the job description, training material, and selection methods.
  2. RECOMMENDATION 2Leverage the materials provided to conduct a C-JAM job analysis for other roles, with suggested edits to training, selection, and job description material.
  3. RECOMMENDATION 3Implement a math test in the selection process.

Provided the client with a full binder (digital folders) of materials and recommendations, including all material collected during the analysis.

04

Deliver

Present to leadership

Presented findings and actionable solutions, including job aids and a math selection test, to the VP of HR and the leadership team.

Conclusion

Job analysis is the foundation. The KSAOs generated from the C-JAM analysis are the most crucial part of this work and benefit training and selection when incorporated correctly. The client received the data and templates to complete this work for successful integration.

Selection
Build the selection process

Leverage KSAO rating scales throughout building a selection process for:

  • Job announcement
  • Interview questions
  • Selection criteria
Training
Build and enhance training

Leverage KSAO rating scales to build new training decks or enhance existing ones.

  • Task statements can be used as content on slides in some cases
  • Consider adding a troubleshooting guide with historical data on how errors were corrected
Outcome / Presented to the VP of HR and leadership team with a full binder of materials, job aids, a math selection test, and templates to extend C-JAM analysis to other roles.
05 · Job redesign

Job Redesign - Organization and Relocation Service

Job Analysis & Redesign

Evaluated organizational workflows and recommended restructuring roles and responsibilities to address workload imbalance, improve scheduling coordination and increase employee retention through role clarity.

Challenge

A small home organization and repair company had concerns with retention, with one person managing two departments.

Approach

Reviewed how work was divided across the company, noting what works well and what may need changing.

Recommendation

Split the Operations Manager role into two positions so each department has focused leadership.

01

Understand the situation

Context and concern

The company is a small home organization and repair business concerned about retention. Its two functional areas, home repair and organization/clean-out, were both managed by one person.

02

Evaluate the structure

What works, what doesn’t

What works well

The company is divided into two functional departments, Operations and Handyman. This division is well done: the relationships between workers and the way tasks are allocated tie workers and workload together.

What may need changing

Given the demands on the Operations Manager role across two departments, it may be more effective to split it into two separate positions that align with the organization’s structure.

Current structure
One role, two departments

A single Operations Manager role covers both departments.

  • Operations
  • Handyman
Proposed structureRecommended
Two roles, one per department

The role is split into two positions that match the two departments.

  • Operations Manager
  • Handyman Manager
03

Recommend

Advocate for the division of roles

Provided recommendations for how a team member could advocate for dividing the roles.

Benefits of the change
  • Better alignment. Responsibilities and tasks shift from multiple people to better fit the organization’s needs and mission.
  • A manageable workload. Each area gets the attention and support it needs.
  • Retention and continuity. The role becomes more sustainable, supporting retention and continuity.
Outcome / Recommended splitting the Operations Manager role into two positions, Operations Manager and Handyman Manager, to create manageable workloads and support retention in the role.
06 · Qualitative analysis

Qualitative Analysis - Digital Literacy in the Workplace

Survey & Data Analysis

Analyzed the importance of digital literacy on employee burnout by conducting interviews and converting responses into 5-point Likert scales. Completed a thematic analysis. Utilized SPSS for statistical analysis.

Question

Where does responsibility for digital literacy fall: on the employee or on the organization?

Method

Structured interviews with 20 working adults, 5-point Likert scales, thematic analysis, and SPSS.

Finding

Some evidence of employee burden related to technology in the workplace.

01

Frame the question

Why it matters

The authors recognize the importance of digital literacy in the workplace: from first-hand experience, lacking it can lead to employee burden. Employers and employees both need to stay on top of technological advancements to ensure stability and growth.

The question became where that responsibility falls: on the employee or on the organization?

02

Collect the data

Structured interviews

Conducted structured interviews with 20 working adults to explore the connections between employee burden, organizational responsibility, and employee responsibility. Responses were converted into 5-point Likert scales.

03

Analyze

Themes and statistics

Completed a thematic analysis of the interviews and used SPSS for statistical analysis.

04

Findings

What the evidence suggested

Found some evidence of employee burden in the workplace with regard to technology:

  • Asking for and giving help. Employees who ask for help typically are not asked for help by others, and employees who help others typically do not ask for help.
  • Rolling out new systems. Brand-new systems or software can be stressful, challenging, and disruptive to normal workflow, but with proper training, support, and collaboration the transition can be successful.
  • Expectations vary. The expectation to know how to use various computer programs seems to vary with the nature of the job and the time period when the participant was hired.
  • Supervisors and technology. It was more important for supervisors to keep up with technology than for employees.
  • Relationship with technology. Those with positive relationships with technology tend to take the time to learn more about it, while those with worse relationships will likely not invest time and energy in building their skills.
Outcome / Found some evidence of employee burden around technology, and that with proper training, support, and collaboration, transitions to new systems can be successful.
07 · Quantitative analysis

Quantitative Analysis - Confidence & Knowledge in Microsoft Excel

Survey & Data Analysis

Designed an assessment that analyzed differences between confidence and knowledge in Microsoft Excel by age, gender, and self-reported proficiency. Analyzed data and wrote a comprehensive report to communicate findings and suggestions for future research.

Question

Do confidence and knowledge in Excel differ by age, gender, or self-reported proficiency?

Method

A designed assessment, with data analyzed by group and a comprehensive written report.

Finding

Significant relationships only with self-reported proficiency.

01

Frame the question

Why it matters

The authors have first-hand experience with differing proficiency levels in the workforce when it comes to computer-related knowledge. Varying knowledge, skills, and abilities are to be expected, but the authors argue that all office employees should have basic knowledge of commonly used Microsoft Office programs.

The purpose was to identify differences in confidence and knowledge with the basics of Microsoft Excel, by groups such as age, gender, and self-reported proficiency.

02

Design the assessment

Measure confidence and knowledge

Designed an assessment that analyzed differences between confidence and knowledge in Microsoft Excel by age, gender, and self-reported proficiency.

03

Analyze the data

Findings

r = −0.735self-reported proficiency and Excel confidence
r = 0.35self-reported proficiency and Excel knowledge
No differenceby gender (female and male) or between ages 18–28 and 29–39
  • Age. No significant differences between ages 18–28 and 29–39. There weren’t enough participants in the 40+ age ranges, where differences were suspected, to analyze them.
  • Gender. No significant differences in Excel confidence or knowledge between female and male participants.
  • Self-reported proficiency. A significant relationship with both Excel confidence and knowledge. Finding significance between this self-reported variable and the tests is evidence of validity.
04

Report and recommend

Future research

Wrote a comprehensive report to communicate the findings and suggestions for future research. For anyone curious about Excel confidence and knowledge, the authors recommend obtaining a larger sample to analyze groups that could not be examined because of limited diversity in the demographics.

Outcome / Wrote a comprehensive report with findings and suggestions for future research, including a larger and more diverse sample.
08 · Climate survey

Climate Survey - Youth Volleyball Program

Survey & Data Analysis

Developed and analyzed post-season surveys to gather player and parent feedback on the program climate, coaching feedback and player development. Recommended head coach align with athletic director to implement mentorship program for coaches, standardize practice schedules and streamline communication for parents and players.

Focus

Program climate, coaching feedback, and player development across a volleyball season.

Approach

Interviews, then two post-season surveys: one for players and one for parents and guardians.

Recommendations

Coach mentorship, standardized practice schedules, and streamlined communication for parents and players.

01

Interview

Understand the program

Conducted interviews to understand the volleyball program and identify what feedback would be most useful to gather. The conversations shaped the focus of the surveys: program climate, coaching feedback, and player development.

02

Create the surveys

Two perspectives

Built two post-season surveys, one for players and one for parents and guardians. Each opens with an introduction and survey tips encouraging honest, respectful, big-picture feedback, and each assures respondents the survey is anonymous. The surveys use a mix of question formats: multiple choice, agreement-scale grids, and open-ended questions.

Player surveyIntroduction, participation consent, and multiple-choice questions
Parent / guardian surveyThe same structure, with questions worded from a parent’s point of view
03

Review the results

Organize and analyze

Survey responses collected into a spreadsheet, with each response as a row and each question as a column. This kept the data organized and ready to review before the analysis began.

04

Deliver to the head coach

Recommend next steps

Delivered the findings to the head coach with three recommendations, including aligning with the athletic director to put them in place.

Recommendations
  1. RECOMMENDATION 1Implement a mentorship program for coaches.
  2. RECOMMENDATION 2Standardize practice schedules.
  3. RECOMMENDATION 3Streamline communication for parents and players.
Outcome / Recommended that the head coach align with the athletic director to implement a coach mentorship program, standardize practice schedules, and streamline communication for parents and players.
